- The firm faces a downward-sloping demand (D) curve and a marginal revenue (MR) curve below it.

- The profit-maximizing quantity (QM) is where MR = MC.
- The monopoly price (PM) is found by going up from QM to the demand curve.
- Consumer surplus is the area above PM and below the demand curve, up to QM.

### (b) Government Regulation
**(i) Per-unit tax and social optimum:**
A per-unit tax increases the firm's marginal cost, shifting the MC curve upward. This reduces output further below the socially optimal quantity (where P = MC), so a per-unit tax cannot achieve the socially optimal output. Instead, it worsens the underproduction problem.

**(ii) Price ceiling at social optimum:**
A price ceiling set at the socially optimal price (where P = MC) forces the firm to produce where the demand curve intersects the MC curve. On the graph, label this output as Qc and the price as Pc.

**(iii) Economic profit at Pc and Qc:**
At the socially optimal price (Pc), price equals marginal cost. For a monopoly, average total cost (ATC) at Qc is typically above Pc, so the firm earns zero or negative economic profit. If ATC > Pc, the firm incurs a loss; if ATC = Pc, it breaks even.

### (c) Total Revenue Maximization
**(i) Marginal revenue after TR-maximizing output:**
At the total-revenue-maximizing quantity, marginal revenue is zero. If the firm increases output by one unit beyond this point, marginal revenue becomes negative, since total revenue would decrease.

**(ii) Elasticity at TR-maximizing output:**
At the total-revenue-maximizing quantity, demand is unit elastic (elasticity = 1). If the firm reduces price by 10%, the quantity demanded increases by exactly 10%.
